reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)

questions.q: The stop sits a few cents under the low it protects, not exactly on it.
questions.why: True. The stop sits a few cents under the low, not exactly on it. This holds whichever low the stop protects. Our scan used 3 cents under the pivot candle's low.
questions.lesson_line: Under the low, never on it. A few cents of room is the rule.
questions.simple: True. The stop goes a few cents under the low it protects, never right on the low.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F62)
which low the stop protects is the held decision D-008 and is not keyed here

questions.q: Where does the originator put his stop on a pivot?
choices: Just under the 30-minute low
A flat 3% under the entry price
Under the 50-day moving average
Under last week's low
questions.why: Just under the recent 30-minute low. On his HOOD trade the stop, 101.16, sat 4 cents under the first green candle's low, 101.20. That is his stop. Ours also sits a few cents under a low, never on it.
questions.lesson_line: The turn candle's low is the originator's line in the sand.

wrong.A flat 3% under the entry price: A percent is not a level. His stop sits just under a 30-minute low.
wrong.Under the 50-day moving average: That is a daily level. The point of the timer is a stop under one candle instead of under the day.
wrong.Under last week's low: That is a weekly level, not a 30-minute one. His stop sits just under the recent 30-minute low.

questions.simple: He puts the stop just under the recent 30-minute low, so the risk is one candle and not a whole day.

reasons: which stop is ours is the held decision D-008; this item asks only what the originator does

questions.q: Our card wants the prior close above the 50-day and the 200-day above the 50-day.
questions.why: False. The card wants the prior close above the 50-day SMA, and the 50-day above the 200-day. The statement flips the second part. The originator describes a stock in a strong uptrend.
questions.lesson_line: The pivot is a dip in an uptrend. No uptrend, no dip to buy.
questions.simple: False. The 50-day must sit above the 200-day, so the stock is in an uptrend.

reasons: a plain restatement of one proposed card line plus the originator's words

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Our card wants the 20-day EMA rising, above its value ___ sessions earlier.
questions.why: 5. The card counts the 20-day EMA as rising when it is above its value 5 sessions earlier. Flat or falling does not count. In IQV the 20-day sat under its value 5 sessions earlier, so there was no daily setup under the timer.
questions.lesson_line: Buy dips in a rising trend, not bounces in a falling one.
questions.simple: Five sessions, because the card wants the 20-day EMA above where it stood 5 sessions earlier.

reasons: +3 one cited fact, the card's rising test (c12)

questions.q: A search for 30-minute pivots finds levels built from last week's high, low and close. What are those?
choices: The floor-trader pivot points
Our own 30-minute pivot candle
The opening range breakout
The hourly Go Signal setup
questions.why: Floor-trader pivot points. ChartSchool says pivot points use the prior period's high, low and close, and on 30-minute charts the prior week's. Ours is a candle you can see: the first green 30-minute candle after a red string. Nothing is computed.
questions.lesson_line: Same word, different thing. Our pivot is a candle you can see.

wrong.Our own 30-minute pivot candle: Ours is the first green 30-minute candle after a red string. Nothing is computed from last week's prices.
wrong.The opening range breakout: An opening range breakout buys the first trade through the 9:30 to 10:00 high. It does not use last week's prices.
wrong.The hourly Go Signal setup: A Go Signal is an hourly close back over the prior day's close by the end of the second hourly candle. It is not a formula.

questions.simple: Those are floor-trader pivot points, a formula from last week's prices, not our turn candle.

reasons: a stable definition on a Tier 2 page, quoted and checked on the page

questions.q: A pivot in a $9 stock that averages $40 million a day passes our liquidity rule.
questions.why: False. Only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. The $40 million a day clears the volume test, but $9 fails the price test. Both tests must pass. Thin names also make 30-minute candles noisy.
questions.lesson_line: Price and dollar volume come before the candles.
questions.simple: False. The stock costs less than $10, so it fails the price test even with big dollar volume.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23), a pair of numbers

questions.story: A leader forms a clean pivot at its 9 EMA on Monday. The company reports Wednesday before the open.
questions.q: Take the pivot?
choices: No; the report is inside 3 days
Yes; a tight stop limits the risk
No; a leader needs an RS of 90
Yes, and sell before the report
questions.answer: No; the report is inside 3 days
questions.why: No. No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. A report Wednesday before the open puts a Monday buy inside that window. A pivot's stop is close, so a gap down through it is likely.
questions.lesson_line: Check the calendar before the candles.

wrong.Yes, and sell before the report: The rule is about the buy. No new buys in the 3 days before a report.
wrong.Yes; a tight stop limits the risk: A tight stop is the problem here. A report gap jumps it.
wrong.No; a leader needs an RS of 90: RS 90 is only the A+ cue. A leader needs an RS of 80 or more, and the story calls this one a leader. The report is the reason to pass.

questions.simple: No. The report is inside the 3-day no-buy window, and a pivot's close stop is likely to be gapped through.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22), a number

questions.q: The originator built the 30-minute pivot for volatile markets, when a position is hard to hold.
questions.why: True. In his words, during volatility it can be pretty hard to hold a position, and that is why he developed the pivot. The card puts it as holding a daily-low stop being hard. A stop under one 30-minute candle can sit closer than a stop under the day's low.
questions.lesson_line: In a choppy market, a tighter defined risk is what lets you stay in.
questions.simple: True. He built it for volatile markets, when a position is hard to hold with a daily stop.

reasons: fixed before: an earlier 'far tighter' claim was removed

questions.q: Candle low 66.08. You fill at 66.83 with the stop 3 cents under the low. How far below the fill is the stop?
questions.why: 1.17%. The stop is 3 cents under the low, so 66.05. The gap is the fill minus the stop: 66.83 minus 66.05. Divide by the fill, 66.83, and show it as a percent. Measure from the fill, not the stop. DK's stop sat this far under its buy.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, then the distance, then the size.
questions.simple: Take the stop, 66.05, from the 66.83 fill and divide by the fill to get 1.17 percent.

reasons: +2 computed key

wrong.1.12%: Used the candle low as the stop. The stop sits 3 cents under it.
wrong.0.78%: Read the dollar gap as a percent. Divide it by the fill first.
wrong.11.67%: Slipped the decimal point one place right.

questions.q: In our rules, a pivot stop 6% away is fine if it is inside the stock's average daily range.
questions.why: False. We prefer a stop 1 to 3% away, 3.5% is good, and up to 5% is acceptable. Past 5% from the trigger, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger. The average daily range does not set the limit.
questions.lesson_line: Up to 5% is acceptable. Past that, wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.simple: False. A pivot stop 6% away is past the 5% we accept, so we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A13, 'usually within about 3%')
the card's hard 3% skip is a number the held decision D-005 still has open

questions.q: Which run of red candles grades highest on our card?
choices: 3 or more clean reds in a row
One very deep red candle
Reds broken up by a green or two
Reds that are still falling
questions.answer: 3 or more clean reds in a row
questions.why: A clean red string of 3 or more candles is the A+ version on our card. The originator's signal is a string of red 30-minute candles in a strong uptrend. It is a grading cue.
questions.lesson_line: A clean string of 3 or more reds into the level is the A+ cue.

wrong.Reds that are still falling: A string still falling has no pivot yet. The green candle must close first.
wrong.One very deep red candle: One candle, however deep, is not a string. The A+ cue is a clean string of 3 or more.
wrong.Reds broken up by a green or two: A green inside the run is not a clean string. The pivot is the first green candle after the reds.

questions.simple: A clean run of 3 or more red candles into the level gets the A+ grade on our card.

reasons: the red-string count is the held decision D-126; only the proposed 3 or more cue is keyed

questions.q: A pivot entry is a market order once price trades a cent over the pivot candle's high, in regular hours only.
questions.why: True. Entries are market orders, and we make no new buys outside regular trading hours. The card's order is a market order once price trades over the pivot high. A buy-stop a cent over it, which turns into a market order, also works.
questions.lesson_line: A market order when it trades a cent over the pivot high, in regular hours.
questions.simple: True, because our entries are market orders and we buy only in regular trading hours.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, E58)

questions.q: On our card, a trigger that comes within one or two candles of the pivot is an A+ cue.
questions.why: True. A trigger within one or two candles of the pivot is a cue for the top grade. It is a cue, not a rule. Nine of the ten scan examples triggered on the very next candle.
questions.lesson_line: Taken out within one or two candles is the cleaner version.
questions.simple: True. A buy trigger one or two candles after the pivot is a sign of the top grade.

reasons: fixed before: it was called a row and a rule, now a cue

questions.q: After your fill, a candle dips toward the pivot low. You may lower the stop to give it room.
questions.why: False. The stop is a real order with the broker, and it only moves up, never down to give the trade room. The one exception is the gap rule, which applies when a gap jumps the stop.
questions.lesson_line: The stop only moves one way: up.
questions.simple: False. The stop only moves up, so lowering it to give the trade room is not allowed.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, D41)

questions.q: Your pivot long reaches 3R the same afternoon, on day one of the buy. What is our plan?
choices: Hold; first sell comes later
Sell a third; stop to breakeven
Sell half; stop to breakeven
Sell it all and bank the day
questions.why: Hold. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. We very rarely sell on day 1 and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. The stop may go to breakeven between 2R and 5R.
questions.lesson_line: No fixed third at 3R. Day one is rarely a sell day, so wait for the push.

wrong.Sell half; stop to breakeven: Not half, and not on day 1. The first sell is a judgment, usually on day 3 or later.
wrong.Sell it all and bank the day: We swing trade, days to a few weeks, so we do not bank the day. The first sell usually waits until day 3.
wrong.Sell a third; stop to breakeven: A fixed third at 3R is no longer the rule. Day 1 is the day we very rarely sell.

questions.simple: Hold. The first sell is a judgment, and we rarely sell on day one.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to ___, is often best.
questions.why: 10R. Selling into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or at about 5 to 10R, is often best. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment: a 3 to 7 day push, or about 5 to 10R.
questions.simple: The first sell is often at about 5 to 10R, so the blank is 10R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E51), which says the ladder is adjustable

questions.q: Bought 238.91 with the stop at 237.09. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 244.37. One R is the fill minus the stop: 238.91 minus 237.09. Add three of those gaps to the fill and you reach 244.37. It is a marker, not a fixed sell level. PSX got there the next session.
questions.lesson_line: Know the 3R price before the fill. It is a marker, not an automatic sell.
questions.simple: One R is the fill minus the stop, so 3R is three of those added to 238.91, which is 244.37.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)

wrong.$242.55: Added three R to the stop instead of to the fill.
wrong.$233.45: Subtracted three R. A long's target sits above the fill.
wrong.$241.91: Added 3 dollars, not three R. R is the fill minus the stop.

questions.q: Account 100,000, risk 1%. Fill 238.91, stop 237.09: the formula says 549 shares. How many do you buy under the 40% cap?
questions.why: 167 shares. The cap is 40% of the account: 100,000 x 0.40. Divide that by the fill of 238.91 and round down to 167. The formula's 549 is bigger, and the size is the smaller of the risk-based size and the cap. A tight stop never justifies a bigger position, because a gap can jump the stop.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop never buys a bigger position than the cap.
questions.simple: The cap of 40% of the account buys 167 shares at 238.91, fewer than the formula's 549.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7)

choices: 549 shares
167 shares
219 shares
418 shares

wrong.549 shares: That is the formula's size. The cap is smaller, so the cap wins.
wrong.219 shares: Took 40% of the 549 shares. The cap is 40% of the account in dollars, divided by the fill.
wrong.418 shares: Used the whole account. The cap is 40% of it, not all of it.

questions.story: Three red 30-minute candles into the rising 20-day EMA. At 11:20 the 11:00 candle is green so far.
questions.q: Buy now?
choices: No; let the green candle close
Yes; the turn is clearly here
Yes, buy half now and half later
No; this setup is already void
questions.answer: No; let the green candle close
questions.why: No. No buying while the red string is still falling, and the green candle must close first. At 11:20 the 11:00 candle is still open. Once it closes green, a later candle must trade a cent over its high.
questions.lesson_line: A candle that is green so far is not a pivot yet.

wrong.Yes; the turn is clearly here: Not yet. Until the candle closes green it can still close red and extend the string.
wrong.Yes, buy half now and half later: Buying before the candle closes is the mistake, whatever the size. The green candle must close first.
wrong.No; this setup is already void: Nothing has voided it. A trade under the pivot low before the trigger does that, and no pivot exists until this candle closes.

questions.simple: No. A candle that is green so far is not yet a pivot, so wait for it to close green.

reasons: one clear card line backed by the originator's words

questions.q: Our card teaches a fixed percent depth for the daily pullback before a 30-minute pivot.
questions.why: False. The card teaches no fixed depth, in percent or in any number. The level decides: with no daily level under the pivot candle, it is not this trade.
questions.lesson_line: Read the level. The average decides where the pivot forms, not a fixed depth.
questions.simple: False, because the card teaches no fixed depth and no number, and the average decides.

reasons: +3 one cited fact, the card's no-depth line (c15)

questions.story: You were stopped on Monday's, Tuesday's and Wednesday's pivots in the same stock. Thursday a fourth pivot prints.
questions.q: Buy it?
choices: No; three tries a week is the cap
Yes; a new pivot is a new trade
Yes, if you cut the size in half
No; the stock is banned for a month
questions.answer: No; three tries a week is the cap
questions.why: No. At most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month on the same stock. Monday to Wednesday used the three. A new pivot is a new trade, but each re-entry counts toward the cap. Pivots fail and re-form.
questions.lesson_line: Three stabs a week on one name. Then let it go.

wrong.Yes; a new pivot is a new trade: Each re-entry is a new trade, and each one counts. Three is the weekly limit.
wrong.Yes, if you cut the size in half: Size does not reset the count.
wrong.No; the stock is banned for a month: The rule counts tries, 3 in a week and 6 in a month. It does not ban the stock for a month.

questions.simple: No. Three tries a week on one stock is the limit, and Monday to Wednesday used all three.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E56), two numbers

questions.q: What is left of a pivot winner is sold on an intraday dip under its trailing average.
questions.why: False. We trail what is left under the 9 EMA for a fast mover or the 20 EMA for a steadier one. We sell on a close below it. A dip during the day is not a close.
questions.lesson_line: The pivot gets you in. A daily close takes what is left out.
questions.simple: False. What is left is sold on a close below the trailing average, not on a dip during the day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E52), a default trail

questions.story: You sold a first piece into the push on day 3. It finished yesterday at 4.2R, and this morning it gaps open at 5.6R, past the 5R mark.
questions.q: How do we treat the gap past 5R?
choices: Sell a piece at the open, always
Sell part or hold; it is our call
Sell nothing until it is back at 5R
Sell it all; the gap ends the trade
questions.answer: Sell part or hold; it is our call
questions.why: A gap up past a profit level at the open is not an automatic sell. Selling part at the open on a big gap is one choice we may make by judgment, never a rule. Holding and trailing what is left is the other choice.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past a sell level is a choice, not a rule. Sell part, or hold and trail.

wrong.Sell a piece at the open, always: The gap is not an automatic sell. Selling part at the open is a judgment we may make, never a rule.
wrong.Sell nothing until it is back at 5R: Waiting for a price the stock has already passed is not a plan. A gap is not an order to sell or to wait.
wrong.Sell it all; the gap ends the trade: A gap through a level does not end the trade. What is left can keep running on the trail.

questions.simple: It is optional. We may sell part at the open or hold, by judgment, but a gap is never an automatic sell.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63)

questions.story: You hold a pivot long bought at 66.83, stop 66.05. A week later it gaps open at 65.70, under your stop.
questions.q: What sets the stop now?
choices: The first 30-minute bar's low
The low of a pivot candle
Sell the position at open
The low of the prior session
questions.why: The first 30-minute bar's low. After a gap against the stop, the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of that first bar is the new stop. The ceiling: if the loss runs past 2R in that time, get out. This is the gap rule, not a new pivot, and the one exception to a stop that only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Two 30-minute rules, two jobs. The pivot gets you in; the gap rule handles a gap.

wrong.The low of a pivot candle: That is the entry timer. The gap rule uses the first 30-minute bar's low.
wrong.Sell the position at open: The gap rule gives the first 30 minutes to decide, under a 2R ceiling.
wrong.The low of the prior session: That is one default for a fresh entry's stop. After a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute bar's low sets it.

questions.simple: The first 30-minute bar's low becomes the new stop, and if the loss runs past 2R you sell.

deeper.trap: The pull is to sell blind at the open or to hope. The rule gives a middle road with a ceiling. One R here is the buy minus the stop, 66.83 minus 66.05. If the first 30 minutes take the loss past twice that, you sell. Check the 2R line before you trust the new stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20), a number

questions.q: A pivot long still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.
questions.why: True. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. A pivot that has not worked in 10 days is dead.
questions.lesson_line: Ten sessions and no progress. The money has better places to be.
questions.simple: True. If a pivot trade is still under 1R after 10 trading days, we sell it and free the money.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33), two numbers

questions.q: Bought 106.65, stop 105.74. The stock trades 110.65. How many R is that?
questions.why: 4.4R. One R is the fill minus the stop: 106.65 minus 105.74. The gain is 110.65 minus 106.65. Divide the gain by one R and you get about 4.4. That is short of 5R, a mark on the ruler where a later sell may come.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R. At 4.4R the 5R mark has not come yet.
questions.simple: The gain from the fill, divided by one R, comes to 4.4R, which is short of the 5R mark.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E51)

wrong.5.4R: Measured the gain from the stop instead of from the fill.
wrong.3.8R: Used the percent gain and called it R. R is gain over the stop distance.
wrong.0.2R: Inverted it: R divided by the gain instead of gain divided by R.

questions.q: The market reading is Yellow. Which pivots do our rules take?
choices: Smaller size, and fewer pivots
Full risk on each graded pivot
Only the A+ pivots; no others
Mostly cash, with shorts allowed
questions.why: Fewer, and smaller. In a Yellow market the guide is smaller and fewer. Green is full risk, Orange only A+ setups, and Red mostly cash and shorts. The reading is a guide, so read the market before the candles.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the candles.

wrong.Full risk on each graded pivot: That is Green: full risk per grade. Yellow means smaller and fewer.
wrong.Only the A+ pivots; no others: That is Orange. Yellow is fewer and smaller, not A+ only.
wrong.Mostly cash, with shorts allowed: That is Red. Yellow still takes some pivots, just fewer and smaller.

questions.simple: Yellow means fewer pivots at smaller size, while Green is full risk and Red is mostly cash.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F65)
+1 fixed before

questions.story: A leader trades 12% above its 9 EMA. This morning: three red 30-minute candles, then a green one, with the stock still 12% above the 9 EMA.
questions.q: What do we do with this pivot, and why?
choices: Skip it; the stock is too stretched
Take it; the candle shape is right
Skip it; three reds make a weak string
Take it if volume rises on the break
questions.answer: Skip it; the stock is too stretched
questions.why: No. We skip a long more than 10% above its 9 EMA. This stock is 12% above, so the pivot is a skip even though the candles are right. A pivot is a dip to the average, and this stock is far from it.
questions.lesson_line: A pivot is a dip to the average. Far above the average, it is not a dip.

wrong.Take it; the candle shape is right: The shape is fine. The stretch is the problem: more than 10% over the 9 EMA is a skip.
wrong.Skip it; three reds make a weak string: Three reds is a clean string, and 3 or more is the A+ version. The reason to skip is the stretch.
wrong.Take it if volume rises on the break: Volume does not change how far the stock sits above its 9 EMA.

questions.simple: No, because we skip any long that sits more than 10% above its 9 EMA.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C29)
+1 fixed before

questions.q: Four pivot candles at the 9 EMA. Which grades highest on our card?
choices: Pullback low, closes in upper half
Pullback low, but closes in lower half
Low above the string's low, closes high
A tiny doji mid-range, after small reds
questions.answer: Pullback low, closes in upper half
questions.why: The candle whose low is the low of the pullback and that closes in the upper half of its range. The card grades that shape best. A weak close, a higher low or a tiny doji after small reds grades lower.
questions.lesson_line: Where the candle closes tells you who won the half hour.

wrong.Pullback low, but closes in lower half: A weak close means the sellers still had the last word. The card wants the upper half.
wrong.Low above the string's low, closes high: It closes well, but the best pivot candle also makes the pullback low itself.
wrong.A tiny doji mid-range, after small reds: A tiny candle after small reds is noise, with a stop of a few tenths of a percent. The card grades it lower.

questions.simple: The best pivot candle makes the pullback low itself and closes in the upper half of its range.

reasons: +3 one cited fact, the card's best-candle line (c14)

questions.q: Raschke's older Holy Grail entry also buys a break of the previous bar's high when price touches the 20-period average.
questions.why: True. Her rule: when price touches the 20-period average, put a buy stop above the previous bar's high, then a protective stop at the new swing low. It first needs a rising 14-period ADX above 30. The 30-minute pivot also buys over a candle's high.
questions.lesson_line: The name is new. Buying over the prior bar's high is old.
questions.simple: True. Her older Holy Grail entry is a buy stop over the previous bar's high when price touches the 20-period average.

deeper.counter: Her version is not the same setup. It needs a rising 14-period ADX above 30, a touch of the 20-period average, then a buy stop over the previous bar's high. The 30-minute pivot adds a red string, a closed green candle and a daily level.

reasons: a web view on a different setup, keyed only as an 'older form'

questions.story: 6 reds into a rising daily average. The pivot candle is the day's low and closes in its upper half. Bought 601.49, stop 595.08. It reaches 0.35R, then the next morning's first candle takes the stop.
questions.q: What went wrong?
choices: Nothing; the stop was the exit
Nothing; widen the stop next time
It needed a bigger red string
You should have sold into the pop
questions.answer: Nothing; the stop was the exit
questions.why: Nothing went wrong. AXON had the A+ shape and every rule was met. Six reds ran into the rising average, and the pivot closed in its upper half. The pivot low still broke, and the stop was the exit. The fixed stop that only moves up kept the loss at 1R.
questions.lesson_line: You will take this loss again. The stop is why it stays small.

wrong.It needed a bigger red string: Six reds is already more than the 3 or more of the A+ version. The candle count was not the problem.
wrong.Nothing; widen the stop next time: 1.07% sits inside the 1% to 2% range the card calls normal. Widening it after one loss would only make the next loss bigger.
wrong.You should have sold into the pop: There is no sell-the-pop exit in the plan. The exits are the stop and the trims.

questions.simple: Nothing went wrong, because every rule was met and the stop did its job of keeping the loss small.

deeper.trap: Judging a trade by its result. AXON met every rule and still stopped out after reaching 0.35R. Fixing it after one loss, say with a wider stop, would break the stop that only moves up. That stop is what kept the loss at 1R.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)

questions.story: Three reds, then a green pivot candle. The 20-day EMA is 262.69; five sessions ago it was 264.36.
questions.q: Take it?
choices: Pass; the 20-day EMA is falling
Take it; the candles are right
Take it at half size, tight stop
Pass; three reds are too few
questions.why: Pass. Our card wants the 20-day EMA above its value 5 sessions earlier. Here it is 262.69 against 264.36, so it is falling. With the average turning down there is no daily setup under the timer.
questions.lesson_line: The timer needs a trend to time. Check the 20-day before the candles.

wrong.Take it; the candles are right: The candle shape passes, but the daily trend fails. The 20-day is below its level 5 sessions ago.
wrong.Take it at half size, tight stop: A pivot in a stock turning down is the wrong trade at any size.
wrong.Pass; three reds are too few: Three or more clean reds is the A+ string, so three is enough. The trend is the problem, not the count.

questions.simple: Pass. The 20-day average is below its level 5 sessions ago, so the stock is not in a rising trend.

reasons: a plain test on a proposed card line, numbers given in the story

questions.story: 5 reds down to a daily average. The pivot candle prints at 15:00 and the 15:30 candle takes its high. Bought 343.15, stop 341.10. The next morning's first candle takes the stop.
questions.q: How do you read the loss?
choices: Allowed, but it is a named mistake
Banned; we never buy after 15:00
A top-grade trade with bad luck
Allowed, and graded like any other
questions.answer: Allowed, but it is a named mistake
questions.why: Allowed, but a named mistake. We have no time-of-day rule, so a 15:30 trigger is not banned. The card names buying a pivot in the last hour as a mistake, because no session is left to work. The stop did its job: the next morning's first candle took it, a loss of about 1R.
questions.lesson_line: Late pivots are legal, but the card names them a mistake. The stop still holds the loss.

wrong.Banned; we never buy after 15:00: We have no time-of-day rule. The clock does not bar the trade.
wrong.A top-grade trade with bad luck: A last-candle trigger has no session left to work. The card names that a mistake, not a top grade.
wrong.Allowed, and graded like any other: The card names a last-hour pivot as a mistake: no session is left to work.

questions.simple: The trade was allowed but a named mistake, because a trigger in the last hour leaves no session to work.

deeper.trap: Turning a mistake into a ban. The rulebook has no time-of-day rule, so a late trigger is not barred. The card names it a mistake, because a last-hour pivot has no session left to work. Here the 15:00 pivot was bought at 343.15 on the day's last candle, and the next morning's first candle took the stop.

reasons: +2 the late trigger touches D-127
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C30)

questions.story: A slow mega-cap: 4 reds down to a daily average, then a pivot. Bought 501.07 with the stop at 498.97, 0.42% away. It reaches 0.48R, then the next morning's first candle takes the stop.
questions.q: What does our card say about that stop?
choices: Too tight; it sits in the noise
Fine; it sits under the pivot low
Fine; far inside the 5% limit
Too tight; skip any stop under 1%
questions.answer: Too tight; it sits in the noise
questions.why: Too tight for that stock. A stop of a few tenths of a percent on a slow mega-cap sits inside the noise, a coin flip. The card names it a mistake. We prefer a stop 1 to 3% away and accept up to 5%. 0.42% is far under that range. The loss was still 1R, as planned.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop is only good if the stock's normal wiggle fits above it.

wrong.Fine; it sits under the pivot low: Under the pivot low is the right place. But a few tenths of a percent on a slow name is a coin flip.
wrong.Too tight; skip any stop under 1%: The card has no such skip rule, and 1 to 3% is only our preferred range. Here the trouble is a slow mega-cap, where a stop this small sits inside the noise.
wrong.Fine; far inside the 5% limit: Up to 5% is the far end of what we accept. This stop is far under it, and the problem is the tight end.

questions.simple: The stop is too tight for a slow mega-cap, so it sits inside the noise, though the loss stays 1R.

reasons: +2 the card names a tiny stop on a slow mega-cap a mistake (c25)

questions.q: The originator bought HOOD at 102.99 with his stop at 101.16. How far below the buy is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 1.78%. The buy minus the stop, divided by the buy. Inside the 3% line, and the trade went over 10R.
questions.lesson_line: Tight risk, a leader, a level. That is the whole idea.

questions.q: The pivot candle's low is 101.20; the day's low is 100.69. Which stop is tighter?
choices: A few cents under 101.20
A few cents under 100.69
They are really the same stop
Right on 100.69, the day's low
questions.why: A few cents under 101.20, the pivot candle's low. A higher stop sits closer to the buy, so it is the tighter one. On HOOD the pivot candle was not the day's low, so the two stops differ. This asks only which stop sits closer to the buy.
questions.lesson_line: When the pivot is not the day's low, the two stops are different trades. Know which one you are taking.

wrong.A few cents under 100.69: That is the day's low, the wider option. It sits further from the buy.
wrong.They are really the same stop: Only when the pivot candle makes the day's low. Here it did not.
wrong.Right on 100.69, the day's low: A stop never sits right on a low. And a stop under the day's low is also the wider one.

questions.simple: The pivot candle's low, 101.20, is higher than the day's low, 100.69, so a stop under it sits closer to the buy.

deeper.example: On HOOD the pivot candle was not the day's low: its low was 101.20 and the day's low 100.69. The originator's stop, 101.16, sat 4 cents under the first green candle's low. A stop under the day's low sits further from the buy, so the same trade carries more risk per share.

reasons: which low we use is the held decision D-008; this item asks only which is tighter

questions.q: Our default moves a pivot's stop to breakeven at 1R.
questions.why: False. Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven at the first trim, not at the first wiggle.
questions.simple: False, because the default moves the stop to breakeven at the first trim, between 2R and 5R.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)

questions.story: DELL, 2026-10-01. The first half hour's high is 543.15. After undercutting its 20-day EMA, it turns on the 30-minute chart, and we buy at 527 with a 520 stop.
questions.q: Which trade was that?
choices: A 30-minute pivot entry
An opening range breakout
An hourly Go Signal entry
A first 5-minute green candle
questions.why: A 30-minute pivot. The buy sat well under the first half hour's high, at a turn near the 20-day EMA. An ORB buys the trade through the 9:30 to 10:00 high. A Go Signal is an hourly setup.
questions.lesson_line: Find the line being bought. The morning high is the ORB; the turn candle is the pivot.

wrong.An opening range breakout: The ORB would buy over 543.15. A 527 buy is far under the morning high.
wrong.An hourly Go Signal entry: A Go Signal is an hourly close back over the prior day's close by the end of the second hourly candle. This buy is a turn on the 30-minute chart.
wrong.A first 5-minute green candle: That is Kullamagi's parabolic-long entry, on 5-minute bars. This buy is a turn on the 30-minute chart.

questions.simple: It is a 30-minute pivot, because the buy came at a turn well under the first half hour's high, not over it.

deeper.trap: The tell is where the buy sits. An ORB buys through the 9:30 to 10:00 high, 543.15 on DELL. The 527 fill is far under that line, so the morning high was never the trigger. Do not name a trade by the clock. Name it by the line it buys.

reasons: the role of the 30-minute pivot is the held decision D-002; DELL's fill under the pivot high is D-003

questions.story: A leader drifts down all morning to its 9 EMA. At 14:00 a green 30-minute candle closes near its high, still under yesterday's close.
questions.q: Which trade is this turn?
choices: A 30-minute pivot
A Go Signal
Red to green buy
Open range buy
questions.why: A 30-minute pivot. A pivot can form at any 30-minute candle, and its line is the pivot candle's high, not the prior close. A Go Signal is an hourly close back over the prior day's close by the end of the second hourly candle. A 14:00 turn is a pivot.
questions.lesson_line: Check the clock and the line. An afternoon turn under yesterday's close is a pivot.

wrong.A Go Signal: A Go Signal needs an hourly close back over yesterday's close early in the day. This turn is at 14:00 and reclaims nothing.
wrong.Red to green buy: It is still under yesterday's close. No red to green has happened.
wrong.Open range buy: An opening range buy takes the first trade through the 9:30 to 10:00 high. This turn comes at 14:00, far from that line.

questions.simple: It is a 30-minute pivot, because a turn candle can form at 14:00 and the buy line is its high.

deeper.trap: A Go Signal needs an hourly close back over yesterday's close by the end of the second hourly candle, from an undercut of a tight hourly flag. A 14:00 candle is too late for that, and this turn is still under yesterday's close. Both are turns, but they do not share a line.

reasons: two proposed card lines that agree

questions.story: Four reds, then a green 30-minute candle. Its low sits well above its daily averages, and no prior low is near it.
questions.q: What is it?
choices: A green candle, not a pivot
An A+ pivot, the top grade
A pivot at a daily average
A weak pivot, just graded lower
questions.answer: A green candle, not a pivot
questions.why: A green candle, not a pivot. With no daily level near the candle, it is just a green candle: no level, no setup. URI had four reds and a green like this, reached 0.28R and was stopped the next morning.
questions.lesson_line: No level, no setup. Find the daily line before you trust the candle.

wrong.An A+ pivot, the top grade: The A+ pivot sits on a rising average. This one floats above every daily level.
wrong.A weak pivot, just graded lower: No level, no setup. With no daily level near the candle it is not a weaker pivot, it is no pivot.
wrong.A pivot at a daily average: The candle sits well above the averages, so it is not at one. It has nothing under it.

questions.simple: It is just a green candle, because no daily level sits under it. No level, no setup.

deeper.trap: The reds and the green look right, so the eye skips the one question that decides it: is there a daily line near the candle? Name the level before you trust the candle. URI had four reds and a green and still failed.

reasons: the level test is the held decision D-125; only the card's 'no level, no setup' is keyed

questions.story: One red 30-minute candle dips to a daily average, then a green one. You buy over the green candle's high at 211.78.
questions.q: What is missing?
choices: A string of red candles
A higher close on the green candle
Heavier volume on the trigger
A second green candle first
questions.why: A string of red candles. The originator's signal is a string of red 30-minute candles, and one red candle is a dip, not a pullback string. The buy at 211.78 came after one red. CRWD reached 1.42R and was stopped the same day.
questions.lesson_line: Count the reds. One candle has not used up any sellers.

wrong.A higher close on the green candle: The close grades the candle. The missing piece is the pullback before it.
wrong.Heavier volume on the trigger: Volume does not turn a one-candle dip into a string. The red string is what is missing.
wrong.A second green candle first: The pivot is the first green candle. The buy waits for a later candle to trade a cent over its high, not for a second green one.

questions.simple: A string of red candles is missing, since one red candle is a dip, not a pullback string.

deeper.counter: A one-candle dip looks like the setup but lacks the string of reds the originator describes. CRWD reached 1.42R before it was stopped the same day. One good move does not make the setup real. Check the string first.

reasons: the red-string count is the held decision D-126; only the originator's 'a string of red' is keyed

questions.story: The pivot candle's low is 142.41. At 11:30 a candle trades under 142.41. At 12:00 a candle trades over the pivot high.
questions.q: Under our card, do you buy at 12:00?
choices: No; the pivot was void at 11:30
Yes; the high still triggered
Yes, with the stop under 11:30's low
No; the new stop would be too wide
questions.answer: No; the pivot was void at 11:30
questions.why: No. Before the trigger, any 30-minute candle that trades under the pivot candle's low voids the pivot. Wait for a new red string and a new pivot. Here 11:30 traded under 142.41, so the 12:00 trade over the high is not a trigger. MRNA was bought at 143.81 and stopped on the trigger candle.
questions.lesson_line: Once the pivot low trades, the pivot is gone. Start the count again.

wrong.Yes; the high still triggered: A void pivot has no trigger left. The high belongs to a pivot that failed.
wrong.Yes, with the stop under 11:30's low: That is a new stop on an old pivot. It needs a new red string and a new pivot.
wrong.No; the new stop would be too wide: Width is not the issue. Once the pivot low trades, the pivot is void and its high is no longer a trigger.

questions.simple: No. Once a candle trades under the pivot low before the trigger, the pivot is void and you wait for a new one.

deeper.trap: The high still looks like a trigger, so the eye trusts it. But the order matters: the low broke first. MRNA's 11:30 candle traded under the pivot low before the 12:00 trigger, and the buy at 143.81 was stopped on the trigger candle.

reasons: one proposed card line with a dated example

questions.story: A leader pulls back for three days into its rising 20-day EMA. You plan to buy over a 30-minute pivot candle's high there.
questions.q: Which is the daily setup here?
choices: The 20-day EMA pullback
The 30-minute pivot
An opening range breakout
An undercut and rally
questions.why: The 20-day EMA pullback. The card calls the 30-minute pivot an entry timer for a daily long setup at a level, such as an EMA pullback. The pullback to the rising 20-day EMA is the daily setup. The pivot is the timer inside it that puts the stop under one candle instead of under the day.
questions.lesson_line: Name the parent first. The pivot only times it.

wrong.The 30-minute pivot: The pivot is the entry timer. The setup it times is the pullback on the daily chart.
wrong.An opening range breakout: Nothing here buys the first half hour's high. It is a pullback to an average.
wrong.An undercut and rally: The story gives a pullback into a rising average, not an undercut. The card names the EMA pullback as the daily setup.

questions.simple: The 20-day EMA pullback is the daily setup. The 30-minute pivot only times the buy inside it.

deeper.trap: Ask which chart picks the stock and the level. The daily chart does: a leader, a rising 20-day EMA, a pullback. The 30-minute pivot picks the minute. A pivot with no daily level under it is just a green candle.

reasons: which setup the pivot name means is the held decision D-002

questions.story: Yesterday's close was 50.40 and its high was 51.10. This morning a pivot candle forms at the 9 EMA with a high of 49.84. You buy at 49.85, a cent over it.
questions.q: A red to green is a different entry. What line does it buy?
choices: Yesterday's close, 50.40
The pivot candle high, 49.84
The 9 EMA at the pivot
Yesterday's high, 51.10
questions.why: Yesterday's close, 50.40. A red to green buys the first trade through yesterday's close. A pivot buys the pivot candle's high, which can sit under yesterday's close, as 49.84 does here. Two lines, two trades, and your plan has to name one.
questions.lesson_line: Same morning, two lines. Know which one your plan is buying.

wrong.The pivot candle high, 49.84: That is the pivot's line, the one you bought. A red to green waits for yesterday's close.
wrong.Yesterday's high, 51.10: The card's red to green line is yesterday's close, not its high.
wrong.The 9 EMA at the pivot: The average is where the dip ended, the daily level. Neither a red to green nor a pivot buys the average itself.

questions.simple: A red to green buys the first trade through yesterday's close, which is 50.40, while a pivot buys its own high.

deeper.trap: Treating the two as one trade. Here the pivot buys at 49.85, under yesterday's close of 50.40. So the pivot has filled while a red to green would still be waiting for 50.40. The lines differ, so the fills and the plans differ.

reasons: +3 one cited fact, the card's lookalike line (c22)

questions.story: Two pivots at the rising 9 EMA. Pivot A follows two small reds. Pivot B follows a clean string of 6 reds, and its candle undercuts the average and closes back over it.
questions.q: Which grades higher on our card?
choices: Pivot B; it has the A+ cues
Pivot A; two reds will do
Equal; both are good
Pivot A; fewer reds, safer
questions.answer: Pivot B; it has the A+ cues
questions.why: Pivot B. On our card a clean red string of 3 or more is an A+ cue. So is a shake: the low undercuts the average and the candle closes back above it. Two small reds fall short of that string. Our LITE trade was a 20-day EMA shake.
questions.lesson_line: On the card, a long string into a shake of the average is the top version.

wrong.Pivot A; two reds will do: Two small reds fall short of the 3-or-more string. The longer string grades higher.
wrong.Equal; both are good: Both may trigger. The grade, and so the size, differs.
wrong.Pivot A; fewer reds, safer: Fewer reds is not a cue on the card. A clean string of 3 or more is the A+ cue.

questions.simple: Pivot B grades higher on the card: a clean string of 3 or more reds and a shake of the average are both A+ cues.

deeper.trap: Calling both good and sizing them the same. Setup grades set the size: A and B setups at normal size, A+ sized up, B- or lower sized down. The card's B- row is the thin end: a tiny midday doji after two small red candles.

reasons: +2 the string cue rests on D-126

questions.story: The market reading is Red. A leader forms a textbook pivot at its rising 21-day EMA.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Pass; we stay mostly in cash
Buy it; a textbook pivot is A+
Buy half size with a tight stop
Buy it, then sell by the close
questions.answer: Pass; we stay mostly in cash
questions.why: Pass. In a Red market the guide is mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day. Green is full risk, Yellow smaller and fewer, Orange only A+ setups. A textbook pivot at the rising 21-day EMA does not change the market reading.
questions.lesson_line: The market reading comes before the candles.

wrong.Buy it; a textbook pivot is A+: Orange allows only A+ setups. Red is mostly cash, so even a textbook pivot waits.
wrong.Buy half size with a tight stop: Smaller size is the Yellow guide. In Red the guide is mostly cash, and a tight stop does not change it.
wrong.Buy it, then sell by the close: We swing trade. A long bought and sold the same day is still a long in a Red market.

questions.simple: Pass on the long, because in a Red market we stay mostly in cash.

deeper.trap: Letting a great chart outrank the market reading. The reading comes first: Orange allows only A+ setups, and Red is mostly cash. The best candle in a Red market is still in a Red market, and a tight stop does not change it, because a gap can jump the stop.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F65)

questions.story: Bought 68.08, stop 66.80, so 2R below the buy is 65.52. Days later it gaps open at 66.10, and the first 30-minute low prints 65.30.
questions.q: What now?
choices: Get out; the loss is past 2R
65.30 is the new stop; hold
Hold; the gap may fill later
Sell half and hold the other half
questions.answer: Get out; the loss is past 2R
questions.why: Get out. A gap through the stop gives the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day the call, under a ceiling. If they take the loss past 2R, get out. Here 2R below the buy is 65.52, and the first 30-minute low, 65.30, is under that. So the new-stop rule does not apply.
questions.lesson_line: The gap rule gives you 30 minutes, not a blank cheque.

wrong.65.30 is the new stop; hold: The first 30-minute low is the stop only inside the 2R ceiling. This one is past it.
wrong.Sell half and hold the other half: The ceiling is a full exit. One stop, one exit.
wrong.Hold; the gap may fill later: Hope is not a plan. The gap rule gives the first 30 minutes, then a ceiling: past 2R, you leave.

questions.simple: Get out. The first 30-minute low, 65.30, is below the 2R line at 65.52, so the loss is past the ceiling.

deeper.trap: The pull is to take the first 30-minute low as the stop and hold, because the rule hands you that low. The ceiling comes first: check the 2R line before you accept the new stop. Here 2R below the buy is 65.52. A low at 65.30 is past it, so you leave.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)
the key is worked out from the story's numbers

questions.story: Your pivot long reaches 2R by 15:00 on the first day.
questions.q: What is our plan?
choices: Hold; first sell day 3 at the earliest
Sell it all at 2R as a day trade
Sell half now, trail the rest
Hold it all; skip every trim
questions.answer: Hold; first sell day 3 at the earliest
questions.why: Hold. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. We very rarely sell on day 1 and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. Selling it all at 1R to 2R as a day trade is a named mistake. We swing trade, days to a few weeks. The originator's quick 2025 exits are an option, not ours.
questions.lesson_line: The pivot is a swing entry with a tight stop. Let it become a swing.

wrong.Sell it all at 2R as a day trade: That is the named day-trade mistake. We swing trade, and a winner can be held longer while it keeps working.
wrong.Sell half now, trail the rest: Not half, and not on day 1. The first sell is a judgment, usually on day 3 or later.
wrong.Hold it all; skip every trim: Holding it all forever is not the plan. The first sell is a judgment into the push, usually on day 3 or later.

questions.simple: Hold. We swing trade, so day one is rarely a sell day, and the first sell is a judgment.

deeper.counter: 2R by 15:00 on day one is when the day-trade urge is strongest. But with a tight stop 3R and 5R come fast. DELL reached 3R the same afternoon and 5R the next morning. DK reached 3R in 6 bars. Even so, the first sell waits for the push.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.story: A leader makes its fourth pullback to the 9 EMA since its breakout. The 30-minute pivot there is clean.
questions.q: How does our card grade it?
choices: Lower grade; the count is late
A+ grade; the pivot is clean
No trade; a fourth is banned
Same grade; the count is moot
questions.answer: Lower grade; the count is late
questions.why: Lower. The fourth or later pullback to the same average is the card's B- cue, and B- or lower is sized down. The first or second pullback after a breakout is the strongest. A fourth is graded down, not banned.
questions.lesson_line: Count the touches. Every trip back to the same average is worth less.

wrong.No trade; a fourth is banned: A fourth pullback is graded down and sized down, not banned.
wrong.A+ grade; the pivot is clean: The candle is clean, but the count is late. A+ wants the first or second pullback.
wrong.Same grade; the count is moot: The card counts the pullbacks. The fourth or later is a weaker cue.

questions.simple: A fourth pullback to the same average grades lower, because the first or second pullback after a breakout is the strongest.

deeper.trap: A clean candle can hide a late count. A fourth pullback can still print a textbook pivot and grade lower. The count, not the candle, separates it from the first or second pullback. Lower is sized down, not barred.

reasons: +2 the count cue is a card proposal, and grades size the position (D38)

questions.q: On PSX the 10-day EMA read 236.78 and the pivot candle's low was 237.12. How far above that line is the low?
questions.why: 0.14%. The gap is the low minus the average: 237.12 minus 236.78. Divide by the average, 236.78, and show it as a percent. The result is about 0.14%. This real day was measured on the 10-day EMA, while our charts draw the 9 and 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: Read the gap between the candle and the line as a number.
questions.simple: The low sits just above the average, and that gap divided by 236.78 is about 0.14 percent.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 the criterion pvt.level is pending D-125; this question keys no line

wrong.0.34%: Read the dollar gap as a percent. Divide it by the average first.
wrong.1.44%: Slipped the decimal point one place right.

questions.story: 5 reds down to its rising daily average. The 11:00 candle is the pivot and the day's low, 237.12. The 11:30 candle takes its high.
questions.q: Which plan fits our rules?
choices: Over the high; stop under the low
Over the high; stop 3% under buy
Over the high; stop in your head
At the average; stop 230.00
questions.answer: Over the high; stop under the low
questions.why: Buy over the pivot high at market, with the stop a few cents under 237.12. Here the pivot candle is also the day's low, so both stop choices agree. PSX bought 238.91 with the stop at 237.09, 0.76% away. Every position has a real stop order with the broker.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, size, trims. Written before the bell, run without a debate.

wrong.Over the high; stop 3% under buy: The stop sits a few cents under the low, not 3% away. Stop first, from the chart; the size comes after.
wrong.Over the high; stop in your head: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
wrong.At the average; stop 230.00: That buys the average before any turn, with a stop nowhere near a low. The buy waits for the trade through the pivot high.

questions.simple: Buy over the pivot high at market and put the stop a few cents under 237.12, the low.

deeper.counter: Here the pivot candle and the day's low are the same price, so the two stop choices agree. On HOOD they differ. The pivot low was 101.20 and the day's low 100.69. The originator put his stop at 101.16, 4 cents under the pivot candle's low.

reasons: +2 the stop choice rests on the held D-008
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F62)

questions.story: Your pivot at the 20 EMA stopped out. The stock then closes under that 20 EMA. A new pivot forms the next day.
questions.q: Take it?
choices: No; the daily context has broken
Yes; a new pivot is a new trade
Yes, with a tighter stop this time
No; three tries a week are used up
questions.answer: No; the daily context has broken
questions.why: No. A daily close under the level the pivot was meant to hold breaks the setup. The 30-minute pivot has nothing left to time. INTC took three stabs in six sessions on a name whose daily trend had turned.
questions.lesson_line: When the daily picture breaks, the 30-minute chart has nothing left to time.

wrong.Yes; a new pivot is a new trade: A re-entry needs the setup intact. After a close under the level, the daily context has broken.
wrong.Yes, with a tighter stop this time: A tighter stop on a broken setup is a smaller version of the same mistake.
wrong.No; three tries a week are used up: The story shows one stopped trade, not three. The cap is 3 tries a week on one stock, and this stock has used one.

questions.simple: No. The stock closed under its 20 EMA, the level the pivot was meant to hold, so the daily setup is broken.

deeper.trap: The tries cap can mislead you into thinking the count is the problem. In INTC the count mattered, with three stabs in six sessions, but the daily trend had already turned. Fix the daily picture first, then count the tries.

reasons: two proposed card lines that agree, with a dated example

questions.story: You bought a pivot at 66.83, stop 66.05. It runs to 19.8R over the next weeks, then reverses and falls back through 66.05.
questions.q: Which plan keeps the most gain when it reverses?
choices: Sell into strength, trail the rest
Half at 2R, rest at the stop
All of it, sold at first 3R
Nothing sold; wait for the stop
questions.answer: Sell into strength, trail the rest
questions.why: Sell into strength, then trail the rest. The first sell is a judgment, often into a 3, 5 or 7 day push or at about 5 to 10R. What is left trails and sells on a close under the 9 EMA or the 20 EMA. It likely left well before the old stop. Most scan trades touched the fixed stop at some point, usually after the targets. What was sold into strength kept the result.
questions.lesson_line: Sell partials into strength. What you sold is what you keep when the move gives it back.

wrong.Half at 2R, rest at the stop: 2R is too early to sell. The first sell is a judgment into the push, and the rest trails.
wrong.All of it, sold at first 3R: Selling everything at 3R gives up the run. The first sell is a judgment, and the rest trails.
wrong.Nothing sold; wait for the stop: A stop hit after a 19.8R run hands the gain back. Sell part into the push.

questions.simple: Sell part into strength and trail what is left, so the reversal does not hand back the gain.

deeper.counter: The scan shows why: 90% of its trades touched the fixed stop at some point in 20 sessions, usually after the targets. Judge a pivot trade by what was sold into strength, not by where the price ended.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook ladder (B19, E51)

questions.story: A pivot's stop is 0.6% away. At 1% risk the formula asks for 167% of the account. A friend says the tight stop makes it safe.
questions.q: What is wrong with that?
choices: A gap can jump it, so cap the size
Nothing; the loss is still only 1%
Borrow on margin to fit the size
Widen the stop until the size fits
questions.answer: A gap can jump it, so cap the size
questions.why: A gap can jump the stop, so cap the size. At 1% risk and a 0.6% stop the formula asks for 167% of the account. The cap is 40%, and the size is the smaller of the two. A tight stop never justifies a bigger position.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop never licenses a monster position.

wrong.Nothing; the loss is still only 1%: The 1% assumes the stop fills. A gap can open below it.
wrong.Borrow on margin to fit the size: The cap is 40% of the account for one position, margin or not.
wrong.Widen the stop until the size fits: Stop first; the size comes from the stop. A stop never moves wider to fit a size.

questions.simple: A gap can jump a tight stop, so the position stays capped at 40% of the account.

deeper.trap: Believing 1% risk is guaranteed. It assumes the stop fills at its price. On a pivot the stop is usually close, so a gap down through it is likely, and the loss then lands past 1R on a position that was sized as if it could not.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A7)

questions.story: Four pivot longs lost this autumn: a last-hour trigger, a tiny stop on a mega-cap, a broken daily trend, a plain broken low. The stops sat 0.42% to 1.72% under the buy.
questions.q: What kept each loss at 1R?
choices: The stop that only moves up
Selling at the first red candle
The 40% cap on the position
A mental stop at the pivot low
questions.answer: The stop that only moves up
questions.why: The stop that only moves up. The four lost for four different reasons, with stops 0.42% to 1.72% under the buy. The fixed stop is what kept each loss at 1R. Setups fail, and a loss at the stop is the plan working.
questions.lesson_line: Losses are part of the plan. The stop is the part you control.

wrong.Selling at the first red candle: There is no exit on a red candle. The stop did the work.
wrong.The 40% cap on the position: The cap limits the size. The stop is what holds a loss at 1R.
wrong.A mental stop at the pivot low: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.

questions.simple: The fixed stop that only moves up kept each loss at 1R, whatever the reason for the loss.

deeper.counter: The four causes were a last-hour trigger (AAPL), a tiny stop on a mega-cap (MSFT), a daily trend that had turned (INTC) and a plain broken low (AXON). Four different causes, one result: each loss stayed at 1R because the stop was fixed and only moved up.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)

questions.story: After four reds into the 50-day, the pivot candle is wide. A stop a few cents under its low sits 3.6% under the trigger.
questions.q: What now?
choices: Pass; the honest stop is over 3%
Pull the stop up to 3%
Buy with half the risk
Use the 50-day as the stop
questions.answer: Pass; the honest stop is over 3%
questions.why: Pass. Skip if the stop is more than 3% away; a risk over 3% is a sign the pivot candle is too wide. If the honest stop does not fit, skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop inside the noise.

wrong.Pull the stop up to 3%: A stop inside the candle is inside the noise. The stop is never pulled in to fit.
wrong.Buy with half the risk: The card's line is the stop distance itself. Over 3% is a skip.
wrong.Use the 50-day as the stop: The pivot's stop is under the candle's low. A daily average is a different, wider trade.

questions.q: The pivot candle's high is 140.33. You look up and it trades 146.30. How far above the high is that?
questions.why: 4.25%, past the 4% line. The move is 146.30 minus 140.33. Divide by the pivot high, 140.33, not the new price, and show it as a percent. Skip it: chasing costs size, not risk, because the stop stays put, the distance grows and the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the chase before you buy it.
questions.simple: The price is 4.25 percent above the pivot high, which is past our 4 percent limit.

deeper.trap: Dividing by the wrong price. The limit is measured from the buy point, so divide by 140.33. Dividing by 146.30 gives a smaller number, which is still over the line here. On a closer case the wrong base would let a chase through.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)

wrong.4.08%: Divided by the new price. Divide by the pivot high, the buy point.
wrong.0.43%: Slipped the decimal point one place left.
wrong.0.25%: Gave only how far it is past the limit.

questions.q: A stock averages 350,000 shares a day. Under our rule of 1% of average daily volume alone, what is the most we can hold?
questions.why: 3,500 shares. One percent of 350,000 is 350,000 x 0.01, which is 3,500. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and the card repeats it.
questions.lesson_line: Check the stock's volume as well as the stop. One percent is the ceiling.
questions.simple: One percent of 350,000 shares is 3,500, the most we can own.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

choices: 35,000 shares
350 shares
140,000 shares
3,500 shares

wrong.35,000 shares: Took ten times too much. Slipped the decimal point.
wrong.350 shares: Took a tenth of the right amount. Slipped the decimal point.
wrong.140,000 shares: Took 40% of the volume. The 40% is the account cap, a different rule.

questions.q: What is the most you can buy?
questions.story: Three limits apply: the risk formula, the 40% cap and 1% of average daily volume. A stock averages 500,000 shares a day. The risk formula asks for 9,000 shares and the 40% cap allows 7,000.
choices: 5,000 shares
7,000 shares
9,000 shares
500 shares
questions.why: 5,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 500,000 is 5,000. The risk formula would allow 9,000 and the 40% cap 7,000. Every limit has to hold, so the smallest one sets the size.
questions.lesson_line: Size is the least of what the stop, the cap and the volume allow.

wrong.7,000 shares: That is the 40% cap alone. The volume limit is lower, and every limit has to hold.
wrong.9,000 shares: That is the risk formula alone. The 40% cap and the volume limit both come lower.
wrong.500 shares: 1% of 500,000 is 5,000. 500 is a slipped decimal, a size you may hold but not the most.

questions.simple: One percent of 500,000 is 5,000, and that is lower than the 7,000 and 9,000 limits.

deeper.trap: Stopping at the cap. The 40% cap comes last in the sizing formula, but the volume limit sits beside it. Here it is lower: 5,000 against 7,000.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

questions.q: Every rule is met. What is the plan?
questions.story: The market reading is Green. A leader, RS rating 88 in a strong group, sits above its 200-day. After 4 reds into its rising 10-day EMA, a green candle closes in its upper half. The next candle trades a cent over that high. The stop is 1.2% away.
choices: Buy at market; stop under the low
Wait for a second green candle
Skip it; four reds is too few
Buy with a limit under the high
questions.answer: Buy at market; stop under the low
questions.simple: Buy at market with the stop a few cents under the low, because the trigger fired and every rule is met.
questions.why: Buy at market with the stop a few cents under the pivot candle's low. A green candle closed, and a later candle traded a cent over its high, which is the trigger. Entries are market orders. The stop is 1.2% away, inside the 1% to 2% the card calls normal.
questions.lesson_line: Every rule met and the trigger fired: buy at market, with the stop under the low.

wrong.Wait for a second green candle: Only the first green candle has to close. The buy comes when a later candle trades over its high, as it just did.
wrong.Skip it; four reds is too few: Four reds is a clean string, and 3 or more is the A+ version. The card teaches no fixed depth.
wrong.Buy with a limit under the high: Entries are market orders. The buy comes on the trade over the high, not under it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B26, C31, E57, F65)

questions.q: What do we do at the open?
questions.story: A pivot long has taken no trim yet. The next morning it opens above its 3R price and under its 5R price.
choices: Take the first third at the open
Wait for it to fall back to 3R
Skip the trim; the gap is a bonus
Sell it all at the open; bank it
questions.answer: Take the first third at the open
questions.simple: Take the first third at the open, because a trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.
questions.why: Take the first third at the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, we take that trim at the open. The hard rule is a third at 3R. Pivot winners often gap through a trim level: DELL, LITE and HOOD gapped through 3R or 5R.
questions.lesson_line: If the day opens past a trim level, take that trim at the open.

wrong.Wait for it to fall back to 3R: If the day opens past a trim level, that trim is taken at the open. A price that may not return is no plan.
wrong.Skip the trim; the gap is a bonus: The trims are what keep the result. A gap through 3R is the trim, taken at the open.
wrong.Sell it all at the open; bank it: The hard rule is a third at 3R, then a third at 5R. The last third trails.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F63, B19)

questions.q: A Go Signal is the hourly lookalike of a pivot. Which line must price reclaim by the second hourly candle?
choices: The prior day's close
The pivot's high
The 9:30-10:00 high
The rising 20 EMA
questions.simple: A Go Signal reclaims the prior day's close on the hourly chart. A pivot buys its own candle's high.
questions.why: The prior day's close. A Go Signal is an hourly close back over the prior day's close by the end of the second hourly candle. A pivot buys a different line: its own candle's high.
questions.lesson_line: Go Signal: the prior close. Pivot: the turn candle's high. Know the line.

wrong.The pivot's high: That is the pivot's line, on 30-minute bars. A Go Signal is read on hourly bars against the prior close.
wrong.The 9:30-10:00 high: That is the opening range breakout's line. A Go Signal uses the prior day's close.
wrong.The rising 20 EMA: A daily average is not the line. A Go Signal is a close back over the prior day's close.

reasons: a proposed card line (the lookalike tell), quoted from the criteria card

questions.story: A pivot long was bought at 50.00 with the stop at 49.40. On day 3 it reaches 51.80, its 3R price, and you sell the first piece.
questions.q: Where does the stop go now, by our default?
choices: The entry price, 50.00
Above the entry, to lock in 1R
The 3R price, 51.80
Lower, to give it more room
questions.why: The entry price, 50.00. Breakeven means the stop moves to the entry. Our rule moves it there between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default. The stop only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: At the first trim, the stop moves up to the entry price.

wrong.The 3R price, 51.80: That is where the first piece sold. Breakeven is the entry price, not the sell price.
wrong.Lower, to give it more room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider. At the first trim it moves up to the entry.
wrong.Above the entry, to lock in 1R: Our default is breakeven, and breakeven is the entry price. It is not a locked-in profit of 1R.

questions.simple: The stop moves up to the entry price, 50.00, because breakeven comes at the first trim by default.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, A4)
